pm_exper_user_4363_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.question: What are some creative ways to spend a free afternoon in the city that don’t involve the usual tourist spots?
pm_exper_user_4363_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.all_options:
(a) Maybe you can take a slow walk around the back alleys and old shophouses to look for hidden food gems and try small dishes along the way 🍢. Sometimes the pushcarts and tiny cafes have the best flavours. Bring a friend, get a teh tarik, and taste as you explore 😊.
(b) Maybe you can take a slow walk around the back alleys and old shophouses to discover small, hidden spots with unique charm 🌿. Sometimes a quiet bench or colourful wall can make the day special. Bring a drink, take your time, and explore at your own pace 😊.
(c) Maybe you can take a slow walk around the back alleys and old shophouses to listen for unique street sounds and record them for a little sound collection 🎙️. Sometimes the mix of chatter, bicycle bells, and cooking smells give a special feeling. Bring your recorder, get a teh tarik from a roadside stall, and just enjoy the atmosphere 😊.
(d) Maybe you can take a slow walk around the back alleys and old shophouses to look for interesting textures, shadows, and street scenes for your photography 📷. Sometimes the little signs and peeling paint tell nice stories. Bring your camera, buy a teh tarik from a roadside stall, and just see what catches your eye 😊.

[] Yes, actually! That mural is called "Kids on Bicycle" and it was painted by Ernest Zacharevic, a Lithuanian artist who was invited to Penang during the George Town Festival back in 2012. The bicycle in the mural is a real, physical one attached to the wall, and the two children are painted in such a way that they look like they're joyfully riding it. The idea was to merge real objects with the painting to make it interactive, so people could pose with it in creative ways.

It was inspired by the everyday scenes Ernest saw while walking around George Town — children cycling around the streets was still a common thing back then. So it’s not just ‘random art’; it’s a snapshot of Penang life.
[] Yes, actually can! On gloomy or rainy days, you can mimic some of the sunlight effects so your brain and body still get that little boost.

One, try bright indoor lighting, especially warm white or daylight bulbs — switch them on in the morning to signal your body clock that it’s time to be active.

Two, play upbeat music while you work. Music can trigger dopamine release, which lifts mood and energy, similar to what sunlight does with serotonin.

Three, keep moving — do small stretches or walk around your shop before customers come in. Physical activity increases circulation and releases endorphins, helping you feel more alert.

Four, wear brighter coloured clothes or display colourful items prominently; visual cues can subtly influence mood for you and your customers.

If you have a spot near a window, spend a few minutes there in natural light, even if it’s raining — it still helps regulate your circadian rhythm.

So even when the sky is cloudy, you can create your own “sunny” environment and keep that semangat going strong.

[] Ah, I know which one you mean — the big one with the old bicycle, right? That spot is actually one of Penang’s most photographed murals. You see, for a lot of visitors, especially tourists from other states or overseas, it’s a way to ‘collect’ a memory of Penang without necessarily buying something to bring home. They see these murals like famous landmarks — a sort of proof that they were here.

On top of that, the street art here often mixes local culture, history, or nostalgia into the design. That bicycle mural, for example, reminds some people of their own childhood kampung days, or just a slower, simpler life. It’s also tied to Penang’s UNESCO heritage status — the street art became one of the city’s ‘signature features’ in guidebooks and travel blogs a few years back, so now people actively hunt for them.

Social media gave it an extra push. On Instagram or Facebook, a mural background makes a more eye-catching post — especially if it’s colourful or quirky. Friends who see it will instantly recognise ‘Ah, that’s in Penang!’ much like seeing a bowl of Penang laksa or cendol.

For someone living here every day, those walls might just seem like… walls, lah. But for visitors, it’s like finding a piece of local story they can stand ‘inside’ for a moment. Kind of like when someone comes to your shop to take photos of your onde-onde or baklava — maybe for you it’s just everyday snacks, but to them it’s something special worth sharing. That’s how the murals feel to some people.
